summary: Describes Media Server Control Markup Language, used with SIP to provide advanced conferencing and interactive voice response functions. It offers an application-level control model, such as between a conference focus and mixer. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A set of remote-control commands for a machine that runs conference calls and phone menus.

questions: how does mscml control a media server
what is the mscml conference control leg
how does mscml use sip info
subtitle: An XML control language, carried inside SIP messages, for running conferences and phone menus on a media server.

tldr.problem: Before MSCML there was no standard way to deliver SIP-based enhanced conferencing. Basic SIP URIs handle simple n-way calls, but not sizing a conference, in-conference voice prompts, or event reporting.
tldr.mechanism: MSCML puts one XML request in a SIP INVITE or INFO message, using application-level objects such as conferences, call legs and prompts. The media server answers with an XML response or notification, carried in a SIP INFO.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Informational. It carries an IESG note saying it is not a candidate for any Internet Standard and was published at the RFC Editor's discretion, so readers should be cautious about deploying it.

today: RFC 5022 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 4722. No later RFC is listed as replacing or updating it. Its IESG note says it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.

sections.title: What MSCML Is For
sections.content:
Media Server Control Markup Language (MSCML) describes XML payloads sent to a media server in standard SIP INVITE and INFO requests. It has two broad classes of function: advanced conferencing (configuring conferences, manipulating participant legs, reporting events) and interactive voice response (collecting DTMF digits, playing and recording media).

The goal is an application-level model that follows the SIP, HTTP and XML development style. It is peer to peer rather than master-slave, so one media server can serve many applications at once. It works with objects such as conferences and call legs instead of raw media streams. One stated use is the link between a conference focus and a mixer in the IETF SIP Conferencing Framework (RFC 4353). MSCML builds on the media server URI conventions of RFC 4240.
sections.eli5: Imagine a switchboard operator who can run a party line. MSCML is the written note you hand the operator saying who to connect, who to mute and what recording to play.

sections.title: Carrying MSCML in SIP
sections.content:
MSCML bodies travel in SIP INVITE or INFO requests. An INVITE that creates or joins a conference MAY carry MSCML, but the initial INVITE that starts an IVR session MUST NOT. All mid-call MSCML payloads go in INFO requests. Because INVITEs often carry both MSCML and SDP, the media server MUST accept multipart/mixed bodies. A media server that does not support MSCML answers an INVITE containing it with a 415.

Two rules keep transactions simple: only one MSCML body may be in a SIP request, and each body holds only one request or response. There are three top-level element trees, <request>, <response> and <notification>, all inside <MediaServerControl version="1.0">. Responses and notifications come back in separate SIP INFO requests. Requests can carry a client-chosen ID to match them with responses.

Clients MUST pick a service in the initial INVITE using a service indicator from RFC 4240: conf for conferencing and ivr for IVR. The RFC explains why it uses INFO rather than SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY: INFO ties commands to the existing dialog, which supplies the context for free. Time values are a number with an optional ms (default) or s unit, plus the words immediate and infinite for some timers.
sections.eli5: The commands are tucked inside the normal call-setup messages, like slipping a note into an envelope that is already going to the right person.

sections.title: Advanced Conferencing
sections.content:
Conferencing uses a star model: signalling and media go to a central media server, which acts as the mixer, while an application server acts as the conference focus. Each caller sends an INVITE to a public conference URI, and the application server uses a private URI of the form sip:conf=UniqueID@ms.example.net on the media server. The first INVITE for a UniqueID creates the conference.

If that first INVITE carries a <configure_conference> request, its dialog becomes the Conference Control Leg. The conference lives as long as that leg does, and a BYE on it ends every participant leg. Whole-conference play, record and active talker reports must run on it. It cannot be created later, and it carries no RTP, so the client sends no SDP or hold SDP. The attribute reservedtalkers caps the talker legs, and the server SHOULD reply 486 Busy Here to the next INVITE.

Per-participant settings use <configure_leg>. Its mixmode can be full (default), mute, parked, preferred or private; other attributes include type, dtmfclamp and toneclamp, and child elements adjust input and output gain. A leg must be parked before IVR commands with prompt content run on it. Video conferencing is video switching: the loudest talker's video goes to the others, and the server MUST switch only on a refresh frame.

Active talker subscriptions produce periodic notifications naming the legs in the mix by SIP Call-ID. Personalized mixes use <configure_team> with actions add, delete, query (the default) and set. Team links are symmetric, and a teammate is mixed in only if its mixmode is private. The RFC's coaching example has a supervisor, an agent and a customer, where the supervisor hears both and the customer hears only the agent.
sections.eli5: A conference is a big room with one controller. The controller can mute people, announce to everyone, or let a coach whisper to just one person.

sections.title: Interactive Voice Response
sections.content:
In the IVR model the media server acts as a media-processing proxy, which helps when the caller's device is a gateway with limited media capability. Requests use the service indicator ivr and MUST travel in INFO. The three main requests are <play>, <playcollect> and <playrecord>. The server does not queue IVR requests: a new one stops the one in progress, and a <stop> request stops it without starting another. A re-INVITE that changes the SDP, such as hold, counts as an implicit stop.

Prompts use a <prompt> element made of <audio> files and <variable> spoken values such as dates, digits or money. The prompt attributes control repeat, delay, offset, gain, playback rate and locale. The older prompturl attribute is deprecated. Servers MUST support file://, http:// and https:// URLs, and a web URL may return a text/uri-list so the application can build a prompt sequence on the fly.

<playcollect> plays a prompt and then collects DTMF digits. Digits pressed early are held in a quarantine buffer, which allows type-ahead. The escapekey defaults to the star key and the returnkey to the pound key. Timers include firstdigittimer (default 5000ms), interdigittimer (2000ms) and extradigittimer (1000ms). Grammars can be maxdigits, regular expressions, MGCP digit maps or H.248.1 digit maps, and a request must not mix them. The maskdigits attribute keeps sensitive digits out of server logs.

<playrecord> plays an optional prompt, then records to recurl. Recording defaults include initsilence of 3000ms, endsilence of 4000ms and a beep before recording starts. Once recording has begun, the server writes media no matter what digits it sees, and the client decides whether to keep the file.
sections.eli5: It is like an automated phone menu. The machine can say a message, wait for you to press numbers, or record your voice, and it stops if you tell it to.

sections.title: Events, Content and Fax
sections.content:
Call leg events are subscribed with <configure_leg> on a participant dialog, never on the Conference Control Leg. <keypress> reports individual DTMF digits, including long presses (held more than one second, or a double of the same digit within two seconds). <signal> reports call progress signals: busy, ring, CED, CNG and a 400 Hz tone.

<managecontent> moves or deletes recorded files. It uses a store-and-forward model: the source must be a file:// URL and the destination an http:// URL, sent with POST or PUT. The source file is deleted only after success, so the client controls retries.

Fax is handled by <faxrecord> and <faxplay>, which exist separately from play and record because the server must speak the T.30 or T.38 fax protocols. Fax record has receive, poll and turnaround poll modes depending on whether a prompt and a recurl are given.
sections.eli5: The machine can tap you on the shoulder when someone presses a key or a busy tone is heard. It can also file away recordings and send or receive faxes.

sections.title: Responses and Security
sections.content:
Every <response> has a request type, a code and a text. MSCML uses a subset of SIP status classes: 2XX for success, 4XX for client error and 5XX for server error, with no 1XX, 3XX or 6XX. Request-specific responses add details such as collected digits or play offsets, and an <error_info> element reports content fetch failures when stoponerror is yes.

The security section says the media server MUST protect the integrity, confidentiality and security of sessions, and that one participant must not be able to tap into another conference. It SHOULD restrict which application servers may create conferences. Limiting conference-wide requests to a per-conference control leg is one reason MSCML is designed as it is. Because collected data can include credit card numbers, the media server MUST support sips: and TLS, and SHOULD support SRTP, although clients may choose how much protection to use. The media management facilities assume a trust relationship between the media server and the file server.
sections.eli5: Every command gets a short answer saying it worked or why not. The machine must also make sure nobody can sneak into someone else's call.
